newsitem.title: USA: Credit card loss rates creep up at U.S. banks.
newsitem.headline: Credit card loss rates creep up at U.S. banks.

text.p: Loss rates in U.S. credit card portfolios continued to creep up during the first quarter, although most banks reported higher earnings that were close to forecasts.

The loss ratio, the amount of card credit written off versus the total portfolio, climbed above 5.5 percent at both Chase Manhattan Corp and Citicorp, the two largest U.S. banks respectively, based on assets.
"I don't think it's possible to know where they're going," said Lawrence Cohn, analyst at PaineWebber Group Inc. But he said it is clear that the direction for the loss rates is higher.

Chase reported Tuesday the loss rate in its managed card portfolio rose to 5.66 percent in the 1997 first quarter from 5.11 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 4.66 percent in the 1996 first quarter. A managed card portfolio includes both receivables owned by the bank and those that have been sold to investors through securitization.

Citicorp, the largest U.S. card issuer, said the loss rate in its U.S. card business rose to 5.91 percent in the first quarter from 5.45 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 4.38 percent in the first quarter of 1996.

Citing Monday's report from First Chicago NBD Corp that its card loss rate rose to 7.4 percent in the first quarter from 6.7 percent in the 1996 fourth quarter, a Wall Street trader who did not want to be identified said there is now concern that the loss rates for the industry will get closer to 8.0 percent before the cycle peaks.
Cohn noted that delinquency rates are continuing to rise "and that's the best leading indicator" of charge-offs.

During 1996, banking officials said there was a departure from past patterns, with some card holders now filing for personal bankruptcy without warning. Many bankers have attributed the phenomenon to a change in the bankruptcy laws and a record level of bankruptcy filings, which last year topped one million.
"Charge-offs are continuing to rise and it's primarily due to bankruptcies," said Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Raphael Soifer.
But Soifer noted that revenues in the credit card business are still strong and earnings cover the credit costs.

On Monday, NationsBank Corp, the fourth-largest-U.S. bank holding company, said the loss rate in its managed card portfolio rose to 6.09 percent in the first quarter from 5.23 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
But a spokeswoman, Susan Carr, said NationsBank likes the business, which remains profitable. Credit cards account for only six percent of loans at NationsBank, she said.

Among those banks reporting Tuesday, Banc One Corp said the first-quarter 1997 loss rate in cards was 6.01 percent versus 6.79 percent in the prior quarter and 5.09 percent a year ago. But a spokeswoman said the first-quarter rate would have been 7.47 percent had Banc One not changed its policy to give bankruptcy filers more time to reaffirm that they intend to continue making payments.

Cohn noted that at both Chase and Citicorp credit quality in commercial lending was exceptionally good. He said while the earnings at the two biggest banks were slightly above estimates, some of the earnings came from non-recurring gains.
